blocks.title: White rust of Indian mustard: the grouped 70:30 leaf analysis, step by step
blocks.subtitle: Which step comes after which, which leaves each step uses, how each step is done, what every table and figure shows, and how to repeat the analysis on a new data set
lines: Prepared for presentation to the Chairman, Advisory Committee
Animesh Panda · Ph.D. (Agricultural Physics) · ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi

Companion to the report ~~Leaf-level hyperspectral detection and severity estimation of white rust in Indian mustard – grouped 70:30 hold-out~~, its Excel workbook and the seminar slides ASD_2025-26_70-30_leaf_analysis_seminar.pptx
Data: 2330 leaf spectra (ASD FieldSpec, contact probe), 48 plots, 4 dates (11 February – 13 March 2026), natural infection

blocks.text: How to use this document

This document is a protocol. It describes the 70:30 analysis of the 2025-26 leaf spectra in the exact order in which it was run, from the raw files to the delivered models. For every step it says which leaves were used, what was done with them, with which settings, what came out and which step used that output next. Every one of the 46 tables and 38 figures of the 70:30 report is reproduced and explained, and four new figures show the data flow, the split search and the inner folds.

The analysis has 16 steps. Chapter 1 shows all of them on one page, with a diagram of the data flow and a matrix of which leaves each step uses. Chapters 2 to 9 then go through the steps one by one. Each step has the same parts:

items: **Step card** – a table with the purpose, the data used (which leaves and plots), the input, the procedure as numbered sub-steps, the settings, the output and the next step, the script, the references, the matching seminar slides, and what to change on a new data set.

**Tables and figures** of the report that belong to the step. After each one an explanation panel gives: ~~What it shows~~, ~~How to read it~~, ~~What we found~~, ~~What it means~~ and ~~Say to the chairman~~.
**Notes** on choices, alternatives and possible questions.

blocks.text: Captions give the number of the item in the 70:30 report (for example "report Table 9"), so the report, the slides and this document can be used side by side. Chapter 10 is a checklist for repeating the whole analysis on another data set (another season, another site or UAV plot spectra), with every setting in one table and the scripts in run order.

blocks.label: Names of the data subsets used in this document.
text: **ALL** – all 2330 leaf spectra of the 48 plots and four dates.
**TRAIN** – the 1631 leaves of the 33 training plots (70.0% of the leaves). Every step that learns anything uses only these leaves.
**TEST** – the 699 leaves of the 15 test plots (30.0%). They are locked away and used once, at the end, to measure accuracy.
**Inner folds** – for the machine-learning models TRAIN is cut three times by plot (GroupKFold(3)): each time 22 plots fit a candidate model and 11 plots score it.
**DL-FIT / DL-VAL** – for the networks TRAIN is cut once: 22 plots (1090 leaves) fit the weights and 11 plots (541 leaves) decide when to stop training.
**UNS-TRAIN / UNS-TEST** – the unsprayed (naturally infected) leaves of the training plots (1379 leaves, 25 plots) and of the test plots (573 leaves, 11 plots); used by the covariate baseline.
**Other splits** – the LORO predictions of the earlier analysis, 20 other grouped 70:30 splits and 5 random leaf-level 70:30 splits; used only to compare designs (Step 15).

blocks.text: Summary of the 70:30 analysis
What was done

White rust developed naturally in 48 plots at IARI, New Delhi, in 2025-26: one fungicide-sprayed healthy block (plots 1–12) and three unsprayed replications (R3 13–24, R2 25–36, R1 37–48), each with three varieties and four sowing dates. On four dates, 2330 single leaves were measured with an ASD contact probe (350–2500 nm) and scored on the 0–9 scale.

The leaves were divided once into a **training set** and a **test set** by whole plots: 33 training plots with 1631 leaves and 15 test plots with 699 leaves. The 15 test plots were chosen by fixed rules (4 healthy + 11 unsprayed plots, all 11 from different treatments, spread over replications, varieties and timings) and, among 5000 candidates, the one closest to 30% of the leaves and to the overall grade and date mix (seed 2026). All feature selection, model choice, tuning and training used the training plots only. The test plots were used once, at the end. This design is called a **grouped, stratified 70:30 hold-out** (Roberts et al., 2017; Kuhn and Johnson, 2013).
What was found

items: **Detection** of a diseased leaf (task A) was reliable: SVM reached macro-F1 0.826 and AUC 0.930 on the 699 test leaves.
**Six grades** (task B) remained difficult: the best model (random forest) reached macro-F1 0.374, but 77% of the leaves were placed within one grade and the quadratic weighted kappa was 0.657.
**Severity score** 0–9 (task C): random forest reached R² 0.517 and RMSE 1.92 grades.
**Machine learning and deep learning** were within one plot-bootstrap standard error of each other; DT-EDNet reached 0.808 (A), 0.313 (B) and R² 0.473 (C).

**Spectra versus calendar**: inside the unsprayed plots a model without spectra (crop age, timing, variety, stage, weather) detected disease as well as the spectra, but the spectra added +0.072 macro-F1 for six grades and +0.102 R² for the score (both real gains: 95% plot-bootstrap interval above zero).

**70:30 versus LORO**: on the same 699 test leaves the 70:30 models were really better in 17 of 30 model–task comparisons, never really worse. Over 20 other 70:30 splits, however, they beat LORO on the same leaves in only 43% of the cases. The gain depends on which plots are drawn, so the honest answer is "only partly".

blocks.text: How to present it

Present the 70:30 split as the main design because it is simple to explain and it delivers models whose accuracy was measured on plots they never saw. Add two sentences of caution: one split gives one test set of 15 plots, so the accuracy carries the uncertainty shown by the plot bootstrap and by the 20 repeated splits; and the decisive test is an independent season or site (2026-27, Bharatpur).

blocks.label: Corrections to the report and the slides found while writing this protocol.
text: **Which leaves trained the delivered models.** Report Tables 45–46 captions, Conclusion 5 and Table 43 (row 2.7.1), and seminar slides 18 and 69 say "trained on all (2330) leaves" or "refitted on all leaves". This is a slip copied from the LORO report. The delivered 70:30 models are exactly the tested models, trained on the 1631 leaves of the 33 training plots and never refitted (code a9_final.py; README of the model folder; report section 2.13 and slide 67 are correct). The captions are corrected in this document.

**Rule for a real gain in the covariate baseline.** Report section 3.12 says that values marked ✓ "meet all three criteria", and slide 21 lists "larger than the fold SD and same sign in all three folds". With one test set there are no folds; the rule actually applied (code a11_covariate.py, caption of report Table 35) is only "the 95% plot-bootstrap interval excludes zero".

**Transfer tests.** Report section 3.11 compares the transfer results with "the cross-validated value". The leave-one-variety-out and leave-one-timing-out tests do not depend on the train/test split; they were run on all 2330 leaves and are the same numbers as in the LORO report. They should be compared with the 70:30 test value (score RMSE 1.92–2.10).

**Two feature sets with the same name.** Conclusion 2 lists the disease-specific feature set of Objective 1, computed on all leaves to describe the disease. The models use the sets selected on the training plots (report Table 26). Both are correct; Chapter 4 explains the difference.
**Report Table 4**: the crop age of the "All" row is 33–94 days after sowing, not 6–36 (corrected here). None of these points changes a result.

blocks.text: 1. The whole analysis on one page

The 16 steps of the analysis are listed below in the order in which they were run. The first four describe the experiment and the data. Step 5 divides the plots into training and test plots. Steps 6 and 7 do not learn anything that the models use: pre-processing works leaf by leaf, and the Objective 1 description summarises how the disease changes the spectrum. Steps 8 to 10 learn from the training plots only. Step 11 opens the test plots once. Steps 12 to 16 explain, check and deliver the results.

blocks.caption: Master list of the 16 steps in run order, with the leaves each step uses, its output and the step that uses the output.

parts: What it shows
The complete protocol in one table: what is done in each step, on which leaves, what comes out, and where it is in the scripts, the report and the slides.
How to read it

Read from top to bottom: each row can only start when the rows above it have produced their output. "Leaves used" uses the subset names of the box at the start of the document; the arrow in the output column names the later step that uses it.
What we found
Only Steps 8, 9, 10 and 14 learn from data that the final models depend on, and all of them use training plots only. TEST appears for the first time in Step 11.
What it means

This is the property that makes the test accuracy honest: nothing the models know – not the features, not the hyper-parameters, not the stopping epoch – was chosen while looking at the test plots (Varma and Simon, 2006; Cawley and Talbot, 2010).
Say to the chairman
"The analysis has 16 steps. Everything that learns uses the 33 training plots; the 15 test plots are opened once, in Step 11."

blocks.caption: Data flow of the 70:30 analysis: which leaves go into which step. Blue = training plots only; dark = test plots (locked until Step 11); green = per-leaf processing and description on all leaves; purple = separate analyses on the same split.

parts: What it shows
How the 2330 leaves move through the analysis.
How to read it
Start at the top box. Arrows show "output used by". The red arrows mark the only route by which the test plots are touched: the 30 trained models predict them once in Step 11.
What we found

Pre-processing (Step 6) and the Objective 1 description (Step 7) use all leaves; Step 5 sends 33 plots to TRAIN and 15 to TEST; Steps 8–10 work inside TRAIN; the deep-learning step further divides TRAIN into 22 fitting and 11 validation plots; the covariate baseline (Step 14) uses only the unsprayed leaves of the same split.
What it means

Steps 6 and 7 can safely use all leaves because they do not choose anything the models use: smoothing and derivatives are computed for each leaf alone, and the Objective 1 results are a description of the disease. Every model input is chosen again in Step 8 from TRAIN only.
Say to the chairman
"Here is the data flow: all leaves are processed the same way, then the plots are split once, and everything that learns stays inside the training plots."

blocks.caption: Which leaves each step uses. D = describe, L = learn or fit, E = evaluate only.

parts: What it shows
A matrix of steps (rows) and data subsets (columns).
How to read it
A blue L means that something is chosen or fitted from those leaves; an orange E means that predictions are only scored; a green D means a description without a predictive model.
What we found

The TEST column contains only E. The TRAIN column contains all the L marks of the delivered models (Steps 8, 9, 10, 16). Transfer tests (13c) and the comparison runs (15c) learn on their own training parts, which are different splits of ALL; they are separate checks and do not feed the delivered models.
What it means
Anyone can check from this matrix that the test plots never influenced the models.
Say to the chairman
"The test column has only evaluation marks: the test plots were scored, never used to learn."

blocks.text: 2.1 Step 1 – Field experiment and treatments

rows: Create plots with known treatments and disease contrast, so that leaf spectra can be linked to disease and to plot, variety and crop age.
Not a data step; it defines the 48 plots used by every later step.
Field 48 m × 24 m at IARI, New Delhi; 3 varieties (V1–V3); 4 sowing dates (D1–D4).

(1) Lay out 48 plots of 5 m × 3.5 m (0.5-m bunds, 2-m channels).
(2) Assign plots 1–12 to the fungicide-sprayed healthy block and 13–24 (R3), 25–36 (R2), 37–48 (R1) to the unsprayed replications.
(3) Place the 12 treatment combinations (3 varieties × 4 sowing dates) once in every block (plot plan in a1_prep.py).
(4) Sow D1 9 Dec, D2 18 Dec, D3 27 Dec 2025 and D4 9 Jan 2026 (50, 40, 30 and 20 days old at the end of January).
(5) Leave infection to the natural inoculum of the season; spray only the healthy block.
No inoculation; crop age at sampling (days after sowing, DAS) is the time variable.
Plot plan (plot → block, timing, variety) → Step 4 (labels) and Step 5 (the split is made by plots and blocks).
Plot plan dictionary LAY in a1_prep.py.
Saharan et al. (2014); Chattopadhyay et al. (2011) for white rust epidemiology. – what each paper did and how its method is similar to this step: see the next table.
Write the new plot plan (plot number → block, treatment). If there is no healthy block, Step 5 splits only the unsprayed blocks.
blocks.caption: Step card – Step 1: Field experiment and treatments.

rows: What they did in that paper (for this step)
How their method is similar to my step

Studied the epidemiology of white rust on Indian mustard (~~B. juncea~~) in India under natural infection, related leaf infection and staghead to weather and defined the temperature–humidity conditions that favour them, for forecasting.
Natural infection is used, and the epidemic is described with their favourable-weather criteria (Step 3).
The aim here is spectral sensing of single leaves, not forecasting; sowing dates are used to create crops of different ages.
Monograph on white rust of crucifers: biology of ~~Albugo candida~~, symptoms (pustules, chlorosis, stag heads), epidemiology and management, including fungicide control.
A fungicide-sprayed block gives healthy leaves of the same age and variety; symptoms define what the 0–9 grade measures.
The fungicide block is used as a healthy reference, not to test control.
Inoculated sugar-beet leaves with three foliar pathogens and measured them with hyperspectral sensors to find disease-specific wavelengths and indices.
Same basic idea: compare spectra of healthy and diseased leaves of known status to find the disease signal.
Natural field infection with six severity grades instead of controlled inoculation.

rows: Crop age at the four sampling dates (DAS)
blocks.caption: Sowing timings (treatments D1–D4 = 50, 40, 30 and 20 days after sowing) and crop age at the four sampling dates (natural infection). (report Table 2)

parts: What it shows
The four sowing dates, the crop age that defines each treatment, and the crop age of each sowing on the four sampling dates.
How to read it
Each row is one sowing timing; the last column gives the age on 11 Feb, 24 Feb, 3 Mar and 13 Mar 2026.
What we found
At sampling the crops were 33 DAS (D4, 11 February) to 94 DAS (D1, 13 March) old.
What it means

Because disease rises with time, a model could look accurate by learning crop age rather than the leaf signal. This is why Step 14 builds a model from crop age, timing, variety, stage and weather alone.
Say to the chairman
"Four sowing dates gave four crop ages under the same natural epidemic, 33 to 94 days at sampling."

blocks.text: 2.2 Step 2 – Leaf spectra and visual grades

rows: Step 2 – Leaf spectra and visual grades
Record, for single leaves, a reflectance spectrum and the visual white rust grade of the same leaf.
ALL: every measured leaf of the 48 plots on the four dates.
ASD FieldSpec with contact probe and leaf clip (own halogen lamp).

(1) On each date (11 Feb, 24 Feb, 3 Mar, 13 Mar 2026) visit all 48 plots.
(2) In each plot select leaves at three positions: L3 and L5 (third and fifth fully expanded leaf from the top) and LL (lowest green leaf).
(3) Clamp the leaf in the leaf clip and record reflectance 350–2500 nm at 1 nm (splice-corrected export).
(4) Score the same leaf on the 0–9 scale (grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9).
(5) Save one Excel file per date: one column per leaf, seven header rows (wavelength, plot, variety, growth stage, healthy/diseased, leaf level, score).
Contact probe: no sun, sky, soil or atmosphere in the signal (Milton et al., 2009). 3–30 leaves per plot and date (median 15).
2339 leaf columns read by a0_load.py → Step 4 (nine L4 spectra removed → 2330).
Milton et al. (2009); Bock et al. (2010) on visual scoring. – what each paper did and how its method is similar to this step: see the next table.
Keep the same header rows (or edit a0_load.py). For UAV data the "leaf" becomes a plot or sub-plot spectrum with its ground-truth score.

Reviewed field spectroscopy: instruments, calibration, contact probes and leaf clips with their own light source, and measurement protocols.
Leaves were measured with an ASD contact probe and leaf clip, so sun, sky and atmosphere do not enter the signal.
Reviewed how plant disease severity is estimated visually, by image analysis and by hyperspectral sensors; showed that visual raters make errors, especially between neighbouring severity levels.
Each leaf was scored visually on the 0–9 scale; their findings explain why neighbouring grades overlap (Step 11).
One rater; image-based pustule area was not measured.
Measured hyperspectral reflectance of corn leaves with southern corn rust at several severity levels and developed spectral disease indices for detection and severity classification.
Same design at leaf level: single-leaf spectra linked to the visual severity of a rust-type disease.
Different crop and pathogen; here three leaf positions and four dates.
Reviewed sensors for plant disease detection and explained how pathogens change leaf pigments, structure and water, and therefore reflectance.
Gives the physical reason why leaf spectra should respond to white rust.

(b) mean grade 1.44 vegetative, 3.48 flowering, 4.47 pod formation.

blocks.text: 2.3 Step 3 – Weather and covariates

rows: Describe the epidemic and prepare the sensor-free information (calendar, crop and weather) used by the covariate baseline.
ALL leaves receive their covariates; only the unsprayed leaves are later modelled with them (Step 14).
Daily IARI observatory data 1 Dec 2025 – 20 Mar 2026 (T max, T min, RH I, RH II, rain, wind, sunshine, evaporation).

(1) For every sampling date take the 7 days that END THE DAY BEFORE the date (no look-ahead) and compute mean T max, T min, RH I, RH II, wind, sunshine, evaporation and total rain.
(2) Count favourable leaf-infection days (T max 16–24 °C, RH I > 97%, RH II > 40%) and staghead days (T max 20–29 °C, T min > 12 °C, RH I > 97%) from each sowing date to the day before sampling.
(3) Compute crop age (DAS = sampling date − sowing date) and the growth-stage code (1 vegetative, 2 flowering, 3 pod formation).
(4) Attach variety and timing from the plot plan.
Criteria of Chattopadhyay et al. (2011); stage code after the BBCH ranges (Lancashire et al., 1991).
One covariate row per leaf → Step 14; disease-progress table → discussion.
Chattopadhyay et al. (2011); Lancashire et al. (1991); De Wolf and Isard (2007). – what each paper did and how its method is similar to this step: see the next table.
Use the weather of the new site and season; keep windows ending the day before each sampling date.
blocks.caption: Step card – Step 3: Weather and covariates.

rows: What they did in that paper (for this step)
How their method is similar to my step
Derived weather criteria favourable for white rust: leaf infection at T max 16–24 °C with morning RH > 97% and afternoon RH > 40%; staghead at T max 20–29 °C, T min > 12 °C, morning RH > 97%.
Favourable days were counted with exactly these thresholds from each sowing date to the day before sampling.
Used to describe the epidemic and as covariates, not to build a forecast.
Reviewed disease-prediction models built on the disease cycle and on weather before infection and symptom expression.
Weather windows before each sampling date (ending the day before) are the inputs of the covariate baseline.
Only four dates, so weather cannot be tested separately from the date.
Defined the BBCH decimal code for the growth stages of crops, including oilseed rape.
Growth stage was coded 1 vegetative, 2 flowering, 3 pod formation following the BBCH ranges.
Forecast wheat powdery mildew at regional scale from meteorological data with and without satellite remote sensing; adding remote sensing raised overall accuracy from 69% to 78%.
Same logic as Step 14: first a weather/calendar model, then the gain from adding sensor data.
Leaf level and one season instead of regional, multi-season data.

blocks.caption: Weather covariates of the four sampling dates (7-day windows ending the day before each date; favourable days after Chattopadhyay et al., 2011). (report Table 6)

parts: What it shows
Weather of the 7 days before each date and the favourable-day counts.
What we found
7-day T max rose from 23.3 to 34.5 °C and afternoon humidity fell from 50% to 33–36%; almost no rain.
Since sowing, D1 and D2 had 17 favourable leaf days, D3 13 and D4 7; no staghead day.
What it means
Infection took place during the cool, humid spell of December–January (last favourable day 4 February). During sampling the weather was unfavourable.
Say to the chairman
"Infection happened in December and January; during sampling it was getting hot and dry."

blocks.caption: Weather of the season with sowing dates, favourable leaf-infection days and the four sampling dates (boxes: mean grade and % diseased leaves); natural infection. (report Figure 4)

parts: What it shows
The whole season: temperature (top), rain and humidity (bottom), sowing dates and sampling dates.
How to read it
Green triangles = days meeting all leaf-infection criteria; dotted green lines = sowings; purple lines = sampling dates with mean grade and % diseased.
What we found
17 favourable days between 18 December and 4 February; T max above 25 °C from mid-February and about 35 °C by mid-March.
What it means
What was measured in February–March is the expression and spread of infections that started earlier.

3. Step 5: the grouped, stratified 70:30 split

Step 5 is the most important design decision of the analysis. It decides which leaves may be used to build the models and which leaves are kept back to test them. Everything that follows depends on it, so this chapter explains it in full: why a split is needed, why whole plots are split, how the 15 test plots were chosen, and how the training plots are divided again inside the model steps.
3.1 Why the leaves must be split, and why by whole plots

A model is always more accurate on the leaves it was trained on than on new leaves. To know how it will work on new leaves, some leaves must be kept out of training and used only for testing. With a single division into a training set and a test set this is called a **hold-out** design; 70:30 means that about 70% of the data train and 30% test. A test share of 20–30% is the usual rule of thumb (Gholamy et al., 2018); Joseph (2022) showed that the best share depends on the number of model parameters.

The leaves of one plot are not independent. They share soil, micro-climate, variety, sowing date and the same local inoculum, and they were measured on the same days. If leaves were assigned to training and test at random, almost every test leaf would have "brothers" from the same plot in training. A model could then recognise the plot rather than the disease, and the test accuracy would be too high. This is called **leakage**. The remedy is to split by **groups**: all leaves of a plot go to the same side (Roberts et al., 2017). For remote-sensing data, Kattenborn et al. (2022) found random splits up to 28% more optimistic than spatially blocked ones, and Karasiak et al. (2022) showed that ignoring spatial dependence inflates the accuracy of classification maps.

Within the grouped design the split is also **stratified**: the healthy (sprayed) plots and the unsprayed plots are split separately, and the test plots are spread over the replications, varieties and sowing dates, so that the test set is a fair miniature of the whole experiment (Kuhn and Johnson, 2013).

blocks.text: 3.4 How the training plots are divided again inside the model steps

The models need more than training and testing: their settings (hyper-parameters), feature subsets and, for networks, the number of training epochs must be chosen from data too. If they were chosen on the test plots, the test accuracy would be optimistic (Varma and Simon, 2006; Cawley and Talbot, 2010). They are therefore chosen **inside TRAIN** with a second, inner division of the training plots, again by whole plots:

items: **Machine-learning models (Step 9)**: inner GroupKFold(3) by plot. The 33 training plots are cut into three groups of 11 plots. Three times, 22 plots fit a candidate model and the other 11 plots score it; the average of the three scores decides. After the choice the model is refitted on all 33 plots.

**Networks (Step 10)**: one fixed cut. 11 of the 33 training plots (chosen at random, seed 42) are the validation plots, checked after every epoch; the other 22 plots fit the weights. The network of the best epoch is kept. For the networks the design is therefore 47 : 23 : 30% of the leaves (fit : validation : test).

**Shortwave infrared, 1300–2500 nm:** controlled mainly by leaf water (bands near 1450 and 1940 nm) and dry matter (Jacquemoud and Ustin, 2019; Mahlein, 2016).

Strongest positive: RVSI (+0.56) and ARI (+0.53). Weak: MCARI, TCARI, PSSRc, GNDVI, CIgreen (|r| ≤ 0.16).
What it means
The best single index explains about 30% of the variation of the grade (0.54² ≈ 0.29). No single index is enough, so a combination is selected.

Say to the chairman
"The best published indices – HI, PSSRb, REP, RVSI – reach about |r| = 0.5; useful, but not enough alone."

rows: Activity 1.2 – Effective ranges and optimal wavelengths (SHAP-CARS)

NDSI and RSI are computed for every pair of bands; the R² with the grade forms a map whose high-value area defines the effective wavelength ranges. Inside them, a gradient-boosting model ranks bands by mean |SHAP| (top 40% kept) and CARS with PLS selects the final optimal wavelengths.
802 correlated bands cannot go into a model directly. SHAP removes uninformative bands before CARS, so CARS works on a smaller, relevant set and is more stable (Ma et al., 2026).
NDSI/RSI R² maps and SHAP-CARS for rice blast (Ma et al., 2026); CARS (Li et al., 2009); SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020).

Threshold R² ≥ 0.5 for effective ranges, else the top 5% of pairs (used here: R² ≥ 0.228); red-edge derivatives 680–760 nm always candidates; XGBoost (300 trees, depth 4, learning rate 0.05); bands standardised; PLS components by Monte Carlo cross-validation (50 splits); CARS 50 iterations × 20 runs; bands kept if selected in ≥ 50% of runs (maximum 15).
Reflectance and derivative bands were pooled in one SHAP-CARS run (agreed decision).
blocks.caption: Step card – Activity 1.2 – Effective ranges and optimal wavelengths (SHAP-CARS). (report Table 15)

items: **NDSI and RSI maps.** For every band pair, NDSI = (R_{λ1} − R_{λ2})/(R_{λ1} + R_{λ2}) and RSI = R_{λ1}/R_{λ2}; their R² with the grade is drawn as a map. Bright areas = band combinations that follow the disease.
**SHAP.** An XGBoost model predicts the grade from all candidate bands; SHAP gives each band its average contribution (Lundberg and Lee, 2017). The top 40% are kept.
**PLS.** Partial least squares compresses correlated bands into a few components; their number is chosen by Monte Carlo cross-validation.

**CARS.** Competitive adaptive reweighted sampling repeatedly fits PLS, drops bands with small coefficients and keeps the subset with the lowest cross-validated error (Li et al., 2009). Twenty runs and a 50% stability rule make the result reproducible.

parts: Why it was done
802 correlated bands cannot be given directly to a model; SHAP removes uninformative bands so that CARS works on a smaller, relevant set (Ma et al., 2026).
What it means
Output: the optimal wavelengths (OW).
Say to the chairman
"Band-pair maps showed where the signal is; SHAP and CARS picked the 15 most informative bands."

rows: Activities 1.3–1.4 – Index construction and ReliefF selection

The best NDSI and RSI pairs come from the maps; the White Rust Index adds a third band to the best NDSI: WRI = NDSI(λ1, λ2) + w·Rλ3. Indices with |r| ≥ 0.95 are reduced to the one most correlated with the grade; ReliefF (classes) and RReliefF (score) rank the rest.

A three-band index can correct a confounding effect that a two-band index cannot; ReliefF judges an index by how well it separates near neighbours of different classes, so it handles interactions and is not fooled by correlation alone.

Three-band disease indices (Meng et al., 2020; Mandal et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2026); ReliefF and RReliefF (Kira and Rendell, 1992; Kononenko, 1994; Robnik-Šikonja and Kononenko, 2003; Urbanowicz et al., 2018).

WRI search: the 200 best NDSI pairs at least 50 nm apart, λ3 every 10 nm, w ∈ {−1, −0.5, 0, 0.5, 1}. ReliefF with k = 10 neighbours, neighbours from the same plot excluded; top five indices kept for each task.
Selected indices (VI) for detection, six grades and score.

Indices are easy to interpret and transfer to other sensors. ReliefF looks at each leaf and its nearest neighbours: a good index is similar for neighbours of the same grade and different for neighbours of another grade (Robnik-Šikonja and Kononenko, 2003). Excluding neighbours from the same plot stops plot similarity from inflating the weights.
What it means
Output: the selected indices (VI) for detection, six grades and score.
Say to the chairman
"I built a White Rust Index and let ReliefF pick the five most useful indices for each task."

blocks.text: 4.4 Step 7 results: how the spectrum changes with disease

blocks.caption: (a) Mean leaf reflectance (± SD) of each severity grade over 400–2400 nm (water bands shaded and kept); (b) first derivative at the red edge. (report Figure 5)

parts: What it shows
(a) The average reflectance spectrum of each grade with its spread; (b) a close-up of the first derivative between 500 and 800 nm.
How to read it
Each line is the mean of all leaves of one grade (dark green = grade 0, purple = grade 9); the shaded band around each line is ± 1 SD. Blue shading marks the water-absorption regions.
Labels at the top mark the regions: VIS (visible), RE (red edge), NIR, SWIR-1 and SWIR-2.
In (b) the tall peak near 700–720 nm is the red edge: its height is Dr and its wavelength is REP.
What we found
NIR plateau (750–1300 nm): grades 0 and 1 are highest (about 0.61 at 800 nm); the higher grades are lower (0.55–0.58).
Red (around 680 nm): reflectance rises with grade, so the red trough becomes shallower.
SWIR and water bands: reflectance rises with grade, most clearly in the water bands near 1450 and 1940 nm.
(b) The red-edge peak becomes lower and moves to shorter wavelengths as grade increases.
The SD bands overlap widely: individual leaves of different grades can have very similar spectra.
What it means

All three expected effects of white rust are visible: chlorophyll loss (red and red edge), structural damage (NIR) and water loss (SWIR). The large overlap of the SD bands is the first warning that individual leaves of neighbouring grades will be hard to separate.
Say to the chairman
"Diseased leaves reflect less near-infrared, more red and more shortwave-infrared light, and the red edge shifts towards shorter wavelengths."

blocks.caption: Mean reflectance at key wavelengths and red-edge parameters by grade. (report Table 23)

parts: What it shows
The mean reflectance of each grade at nine key wavelengths and the two red-edge parameters, with the change from grade 0 to grade 9.
How to read it
The last column gives the percentage change between grade 0 and grade 9 (for REP, the change in nm).
What we found
Largest relative increases: 1940 nm water band (+66%), 1450 nm water band (+49%), 680 nm red (+45%) and 2200 nm (+34%).
Decreases: 760 nm (−11%) and 800 nm (−9.5%) on the NIR plateau; Dr −16%.
REP falls from 709.0 nm (grade 0) to 701.3 nm (grade 9): a blue shift of 7.7 nm, almost step by step (708.5, 705.2, 703.5, 701.8 nm for grades 1–7).
The green band (550 nm) hardly changes (+6%).
What it means

The red-edge position is the most regular indicator: it moves monotonically with grade. The water bands show the largest relative change, which supports keeping them in the analysis of contact-probe data. A blue shift of this size (about 8 nm) is typical of chlorophyll loss in diseased leaves (Mahlein et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2020).
Say to the chairman
"The red-edge position moves 7.7 nm from 709 to 701 nm between healthy and grade-9 leaves, and the water bands change by 50–66%."

blocks.caption: First derivative of the mean spectra of each grade over 400–2400 nm. (report Figure 6)

parts: What it shows
The slope of the mean spectrum of each grade across the full range.
How to read it
Positive values mean reflectance is rising with wavelength, negative values that it is falling. Peaks mark the steepest parts of the spectrum.
What we found
The red-edge peak near 720 nm is by far the largest and is lower for higher grades.
Smaller differences appear at the green peak (around 520–570 nm), at the edges of the water bands (near 1380, 1450, 1870 nm) and in the SWIR-2.
What it means

The derivative turns small changes of shape into visible peaks. It shows that the disease signal is not only in the red edge: the flanks of the water bands also respond, which is why derivative bands from the NIR and SWIR are selected later.
Say to the chairman
"The derivative makes the red edge and the water-band edges stand out; both respond to the disease."

blocks.caption: Mean reflectance by grade within each growth stage. (report Figure 7)

parts: What it shows
The mean spectra of each grade drawn separately for the vegetative, flowering and pod-formation stages.
How to read it
Compare the lines within one panel (the grade effect at a given stage) and between panels (the stage effect).
What we found
Vegetative (n = 555): the grade lines almost coincide; these leaves are mostly grade 0–1, so there is little disease to see.
Flowering (n = 1160): a clear grade effect – NIR falls and SWIR rises with grade.
Pod formation (n = 615): SWIR and the water bands rise strongly with grade; on the NIR plateau the higher grades are slightly **higher**, the opposite of flowering.
What it means

The SWIR/water-band increase is consistent wherever there is disease, but the direction of the NIR change depends on the stage. This is an important caution: NIR reflectance on its own is not a stable disease indicator, because leaf ageing and canopy development also change it. Indicators based on the red edge and the water bands are more robust.
Caution
Growth stage and date are linked in this design (vegetative leaves only on the first two dates, pod formation only on the last two), so stage effects cannot be separated from date effects.
Say to the chairman
"The water-band signal is present at every stage with disease; the near-infrared change depends on the stage, so it is not a reliable indicator on its own."

blocks.caption: Mean leaf grade (± 95% confidence interval) by growth stage, variety, leaf position and sowing timing. (report Figure 8)

parts: What it shows
The average grade in each level of four factors, with 95% confidence intervals.
How to read it
Bar height = mean grade; the error bar = 95% confidence interval; n = number of leaves. Non-overlapping error bars indicate a clear difference.
What we found
Growth stage: vegetative 1.44, flowering 3.48, pod formation 4.47.
Variety: V1 3.45, V2 3.37, V3 2.96 – V3 had somewhat less disease.
Leaf position: L3 2.59, L5 3.35, LL 4.07 – disease increases down the plant.
What it means

The large stage differences mostly reflect the date (later dates = later stages = more disease). Leaf position is a genuine within-date effect: the lower leaves carry more disease. The variety and timing differences are smaller; the covariate model (Step 14) shows that, at the same crop age, the late sowing D4 actually had more disease.
Say to the chairman
"Disease increased with stage and down the plant; V3 had the least disease."

blocks.caption: Pearson correlation of reflectance and first derivative with the leaf grade (dotted lines: |r| = 0.3). (report Figure 9)

parts: What it shows
For every wavelength, how strongly reflectance (blue) and its first derivative (red) follow the grade across all 2330 leaves.
How to read it

The curve gives r at each wavelength; above zero means the value rises with grade, below zero that it falls. Dotted lines at ±0.3 mark a moderate correlation. The two circles mark the strongest values.
What we found
Reflectance peaks at 695 nm (r = +0.46): red reflectance rises with disease. It is negative across the NIR (about −0.3 to −0.4) and positive in the SWIR (up to about +0.38).
The derivative reaches r = +0.62 at 800 nm (just beyond the red edge) and −0.56 at 720 nm (on the red-edge peak).
The derivative curve changes sign many times; reflectance changes smoothly.
What it means

The first derivative carries a stronger disease signal than reflectance (0.62 vs 0.46). The opposite signs at 720 and 800 nm describe the same event: the red-edge peak becomes lower and shifts to shorter wavelengths, so the slope falls at 720 nm and rises at 800 nm. This explains why derivative bands dominate the selected features.
Say to the chairman
"The derivative at 800 nm is the single best indicator (r = 0.62); the derivative is consistently stronger than plain reflectance."

blocks.text: 4.5 Step 7 results: effective ranges and optimal wavelengths

blocks.caption: R² of (a) NDSI and (b) RSI with the leaf grade for all band pairs (white contour: effective-range threshold; star: best pair). (report Figure 10)

parts: What it shows
For every combination of two wavelengths, how well the normalised difference (a) or ratio (b) of those two bands predicts the grade.
How to read it

Each point of the map is one band pair (λ_{1} on the horizontal axis, λ_{2} on the vertical). Colour = R² with the grade (dark blue 0, dark red 0.36). The maps are symmetric about the diagonal. The white contour encloses the top 5% of pairs (R² ≥ 0.23); the star marks the best pair.
What we found
No pair reached the planned threshold of R² = 0.5; the best was **(795, 805) nm with R² = 0.36** for both NDSI and RSI.
The highest values form a narrow corner where one band lies in the visible/red edge and the other on the NIR shoulder (around 750–850 nm), and a second area within the SWIR (1400–1900 nm).
The effective ranges defined by the contour were 515–1365, 1380–1395, 1405–1895 and 2020–2105 nm (292 bands at 5-nm spacing).
What it means

Two-band indices capture at most about a third of the variation in leaf grade. The best pair is two very close bands on the NIR shoulder – in effect a measure of the slope there, which links it directly to the derivative at 800 nm. Because no pair reached R² 0.5, the fall-back rule (top 5%) was used, as planned in the methodology.
Say to the chairman
"The best two-band index is NDSI(795, 805) with R² 0.36; the useful band pairs lie at the red edge–NIR shoulder and in the shortwave infrared."

blocks.caption: SHAP-CARS: (a) SHAP importance of all candidate bands, (b) choice of PLS components, (c) one CARS run, (d) selection frequency over 20 runs. (report Figure 11)

parts: What it shows
The four stages of the band selection.
How to read it
(a) Mean |SHAP| of each candidate band (red = derivative, blue = reflectance); the dashed line marks the top-40% cut.
(b) Cross-validated error (RMSE) of PLS against the number of components; the red line marks the number chosen.
(c) One CARS run: black = number of bands still kept, red = cross-validated error; the dotted line marks the iteration with the lowest error.
(d) How often each band was selected in 20 CARS runs; the dashed line marks 50%.
What we found
(a) The largest SHAP values are derivative bands near 680–870 nm and near 1800 nm; reflectance bands contribute little.
(b) The error fell steadily up to 15 components, so 15 were used.
(c) CARS reduced about 110 bands to a few dozen within the first iterations; the error was lowest early (around iteration 5) and rose when too many bands were removed.
(d) Twenty-three bands were selected in at least 70% of runs; the 15 most frequent (FD1090 and FD565 in every run) were kept, all of them derivatives.
What it means

The model-based selection agrees with the correlation curves: the derivative carries the information. Repeating CARS 20 times and keeping only frequently chosen bands protects against the randomness of a single run.
Say to the chairman
"SHAP removed the uninformative bands, CARS chose the best combination, and over 20 runs 15 derivative bands were chosen consistently."

blocks.caption: Optimal wavelengths selected by SHAP-CARS on all leaves. (report Table 24)

parts: What it shows
The 15 optimal wavelengths with their type, spectral region, CARS selection frequency and SHAP importance.
How to read it
"CARS frequency" = share of the 20 runs in which the band was selected; "mean |SHAP|" = its average contribution to the XGBoost predictions.
What we found
All 15 are first-derivative bands: 4 in the visible (FD550, FD565, FD595, FD665), 10 in the NIR (760–1245 nm) and 1 in the SWIR (FD1660).
The bands with the largest SHAP values are FD860 (0.110), FD810 (0.106) and FD1060 (0.089); FD1090 and FD565 were chosen in every run.
What it means

The selected bands cover the green peak and red absorption (pigments), the NIR shoulder and plateau (structure) and one SWIR band (water/dry matter). A high CARS frequency and a high SHAP value are different things: a band can be chosen often because it adds unique information even if its average contribution is small.
Say to the chairman
"Fifteen derivative bands were chosen – mostly on the NIR shoulder, plus green, red and one shortwave-infrared band."

blocks.caption: Optimal wavelengths marked on the mean reflectance (a) and first-derivative (b) spectra. (report Figure 12)

parts: What it shows
Where the 15 selected bands lie on the average spectrum.
How to read it
Red vertical lines mark the selected wavelengths; panel (a) has none because no reflectance band was selected.
What we found
The lines cluster around the green peak (550–595 nm), the red absorption (665 nm), the red-edge shoulder and NIR (760–1090 nm), with single bands at 1245 and 1660 nm.
What it means

The selection is physically sensible: it picks the slopes on both sides of the green peak, the red edge and the NIR plateau, and the flank of the 1450-nm water band. These are the regions a UAV hyperspectral camera must cover.
Say to the chairman
"The chosen bands sit exactly on the parts of the spectrum that respond to chlorophyll, leaf structure and water."

blocks.text: 4.6 Step 7 results: indices and the disease-specific feature set

blocks.caption: White Rust Index (WRI) by grade: (a) distributions, (b) all leaves with mean ± SD. (report Figure 13)

parts: What it shows
The best three-band index found by the search, and how its value changes with grade.
How to read it
(a) Violin and box plots of the index for each grade; (b) every leaf as a dot (slightly spread sideways), with the mean ± SD per grade in black.
What we found
The search returned WRI = NDSI(780, 830) with a third-band weight w = 0, i.e. the third band (400 nm) adds nothing. Correlation with grade r = −0.59.
The mean WRI falls steadily from about +0.003 (grade 0) to about −0.007 (grade 9), but the spread within each grade is large and the distributions overlap.
The next best candidates were almost identical (|r| 0.592–0.595).
What it means

For leaf spectra, a third band did not improve the best two-band contrast: the NIR-shoulder slope already carries the signal. The index orders the grades correctly on average, but a single leaf cannot be graded from it reliably because of the overlap.
Say to the chairman
"A three-band White Rust Index did not beat the two-band NIR-shoulder index; it ranks grades on average, but leaves overlap."

blocks.caption: Correlation among the indices kept after the |r| ≥ 0.95 filter. (report Figure 14)

parts: What it shows
How the 23 remaining indices correlate with each other.
How to read it
Each cell is the correlation between two indices: dark red = +1, dark blue = −1, white = 0.
What we found
The redundancy filter reduced 47 index features (41 published, 3 red-edge parameters, 3 data-driven) to 23.
A large block of greenness and red-edge indices (RSI_best, HI, PSSR, REP, NDVI850, RDVI, PRI, MTVI2) still correlate at 0.7–0.9 with each other.
DWSI-2, MCARI, PSSRc and TCARI are only weakly related to the others.
What it means

Even after removing near-duplicates, many indices measure almost the same thing (greenness and the red edge). The few independent indices (DWSI-2, MCARI) are valuable because they add different information, which is exactly what ReliefF and the VIF check reward.
Say to the chairman
"Most indices tell the same greenness story; only a few, like DWSI-2, add something different."

blocks.caption: ReliefF weights of the indices for detection and six grades, and RReliefF weights for the score (dark blue: top five, selected). (report Figure 15)

parts: What it shows
The ranking of the indices by ReliefF for each task.
How to read it
Longer bar = more useful for separating neighbouring leaves of different classes (or different scores). Dark blue bars are the five selected.
What we found
Detection: RSI_best, HI, REP, RVSI, DWSI-2.
Six grades: REP, RSI_best, HI, DWSI-2, RVSI.
Score: RSI_best, HI, MCARI, PRI, Dr.
What it means

The same core – the best data-driven ratio (RSI_best), the Healthy Index (HI) and the red-edge position (REP) – is chosen for all tasks, supported by the disease–water stress index DWSI-2 and the red-edge stress index RVSI. For the score, pigment indices (MCARI, PRI) and the red-edge height (Dr) enter.
Say to the chairman
"ReliefF picked the same core indices for all three tasks: the NIR-shoulder ratio, the Healthy Index and the red-edge position."

blocks.caption: Variance inflation factors of the disease-specific feature set. (report Figure 16)

parts: What it shows
The 11 features left after the variance-inflation check and their VIF.
How to read it
Red = derivative band, green = vegetation index; the dashed line is the limit of 10.
What we found

Twelve features were removed in turn because they overlapped with others, the largest first: FD855 (VIF 119), PRI (93), FD565 (91), FD810 (75), then FD860, RVSI, FD830, RSI_best, FD1660, HI, FD915, MCARI.

blocks.text: 5. Step 8: feature selection on the training plots

Step 8 is where the analysis starts to learn for the models. It repeats the whole Objective 1 selection chain of Step 7, but only on the 1631 leaves of the 33 training plots. Its output – one feature set per task – is the only input the models of Steps 9 and 10 receive. Because the test plots were not used, the selection cannot have been influenced by them. Choosing features on all data and then testing on part of the same data is a well-known source of optimistic accuracy (Ambroise and McLachlan, 2002).

(1) Standardise: mean and SD of each feature from the 1631 training leaves; apply the same numbers to training and test leaves.

(5) Grid search (GridSearchCV) on that subset with the same three inner folds.
(6) Refit the best setting on all 1631 training leaves (class weights balanced; XGBoost with balanced sample weights).
(7) Predict the 699 test leaves once (class or score; probability or decision value for AUC).
(8) Save model, feature list, scaler and settings (joblib).

blocks.label: A small detail an examiner may ask about.
blocks.text: The scaler (mean and SD) was computed once from all 1631 training leaves and then used inside the inner folds. explained variance, root mean square and mean absolute error (grade units)
SD of observed / RMSE; > 2 good, 1.4–2 fair, < 1.4 poor (Williams, 2001)
blocks.caption: Evaluation metrics. (report Table 20)

parts: What it shows
Every metric used, its formula and the task it serves.
How to read it

Macro-F1 = mean of the F1 of each class, so the rare grade 9 counts as much as grade 0. QWK gives partial credit to near misses: confusing grade 3 with 5 costs less than 0 with 9. RPD = SD of the observed grades / RMSE.
What it means
No single number describes a model. Detection needs both sensitivity and specificity; grades need an exact metric (macro-F1) and an ordinal one (QWK); the score needs error in grade units (RMSE).
Say to the chairman
"Macro-F1 is the main metric for classes, R² and RMSE for the score; QWK tells how far off the wrong grades are."

blocks.label: Why a bootstrap of whole plots?
blocks.text: With one test set there are no folds to give a spread. The test leaves of one plot are related, so resampling single leaves would make the interval too narrow. Resampling whole plots keeps each plot's leaves together, as the split did (Field and Welsh, 2007). Resampling healthy and unsprayed plots separately keeps the test set's mix of 4 healthy and 11 unsprayed plots in every resample.

blocks.caption: Task A – detection: test metrics (test plots of the 70:30 split; n = 699 test leaves). (report Table 29)

parts: What it shows
Detection results of all ten model types on the 699 test leaves, best first.
How to read it
"± bootstrap SE" is the plot-bootstrap standard error. Sensitivity = share of diseased leaves found; specificity = share of healthy leaves called healthy.
What we found
SVM was best: macro-F1 0.826 ± 0.017, AUC 0.930, sensitivity 0.843, specificity 0.900 (153 of 170 healthy and 446 of 529 diseased test leaves correct).
DNN-F1 (0.824), ResNet18 (0.822), ConvNeXt V2-Atto (0.818), XGBoost (0.813), RF (0.811) and DT-EDNet (0.808) were within one standard error of SVM.
Several networks reached high sensitivity (0.89–0.92) but low specificity (0.70–0.77): they called too many healthy leaves diseased. PLS-DA was weakest (0.719).
What it means
Detection is reliable and does not need a deep network. The differences among the top seven models are smaller than the uncertainty of the test set.
Say to the chairman
"On plots it never saw, SVM detects a diseased leaf with macro-F1 0.83 and AUC 0.93; the next six models are statistically as good."

blocks.caption: Task B – six grades: test metrics and F1 of each grade. (report Table 30)

parts: What it shows
Six-grade results with the F1 of each grade.
How to read it
OA and macro-F1 count exact hits; QWK and "±1 grade" give credit for near misses.
What we found
RF was best by macro-F1 (0.374; QWK 0.657; 77.3% within one grade); SVM had the highest OA (0.418) and QWK (0.658).
Grade 0 was recognised best (F1 0.54–0.76); grades 3 (0.00–0.30) and 9 (0.00–0.31) worst. PLS-DA never predicted grades 3, 7 or 9 correctly (F1 0.00).
What it means
The exact grade is right for only about 40% of leaves, but three in four leaves are within one grade. The spectral signal ranks severity but cannot separate neighbouring grades sharply.
Say to the chairman
"Exact six-grade accuracy is about 40%, but three quarters of leaves are within one grade."

blocks.caption: Task C – severity score: test metrics (grade units). (report Table 31)

parts: What it shows
Severity-score results of all models.
What we found

RF (R² 0.517, RMSE 1.919 ± 0.115) and XGBoost (0.512) were best; DNN-F1 was the best network (0.481). RPD of the best models 1.43–1.44 ("fair"); bias −0.1 to −0.2 grades. EfficientNet-B0 was weakest (R² 0.287, bias −0.61).
What it means
The score explains about half of the variation in grade with a typical error of about two grades. It is useful for ranking leaves and plots, not for exact grading.
Say to the chairman
"The best score model explains 52% of the variation with an error of 1.9 grades."

blocks.caption: Model comparison on the 70:30 test plots: macro-F1 for detection and six grades (± plot-bootstrap SE) and R² for the severity score (blue: machine learning; purple: deep learning). (report Figure 21)

parts: What it shows
The main metric of all models for the three tasks.
How to read it
Bars sorted from best to worst; blue = machine learning, purple = deep learning; whiskers = plot-bootstrap SE.
What we found
In every task the whiskers of the top models overlap. Tree ensembles and SVM lead; DT-EDNet is in the middle (score) or lower half (detection, six grades).
What it means
The choice between ML and DL matters less than the choice of features and the difficulty of the task.
Say to the chairman
"Machine learning and deep learning overlap; no model is clearly best."

blocks.caption: All metrics of all models (darker = better within each column). (report Figure 22)

parts: What it shows
Every metric of every model as a colour table.
How to read it
Darker green = better within the column (lower is better for RMSE and MAE). Read along a row for a model's profile.
What we found
Rows of SVM, RF and XGBoost are dark across tasks; EfficientNet-B0 and PLS are light in most columns.
What it means
Good models are good across metrics, so the ranking does not depend on the choice of metric.
Say to the chairman
"The same few models are good on every metric."

blocks.caption: Confusion matrices (counts and row percentages) of the best machine-learning and deep-learning models for six grades. (report Figure 23)

parts: What it shows
For the best ML model (RF) and the best network (ConvNeXt V2-Atto), how the test leaves of each true grade were classified.
How to read it
Rows = true grade, columns = predicted grade; each cell gives count and row percentage; the diagonal is correct.
What we found
RF classified 75% of grade-0 leaves correctly, 41% of grade 1, 19% of grade 3, 33% of grade 5, 28% of grade 7 and 33% of grade 9; most errors fall in the cells next to the diagonal.
What it means
Errors are mostly one grade away, which is why QWK (0.66) is much higher than macro-F1 (0.37).
Say to the chairman
"The models confuse neighbouring grades, not distant ones."

blocks.caption: ROC curves for detection (solid: machine learning; dashed: deep learning). (report Figure 24)

parts: What it shows
Sensitivity against false-positive rate for all detection models as the threshold changes.
How to read it
Curves closer to the upper-left corner are better; the area under each curve is the AUC.
What we found
Most curves lie close together with AUC 0.87–0.93; PLS-DA (0.825) lies lowest.
What it means
A threshold can be chosen to favour sensitivity (early warning) or specificity (fewer false alarms) without retraining.
Say to the chairman
"All good models separate healthy and diseased leaves with AUC around 0.9."

blocks.caption: Six-grade performance profile (F1 of each grade, OA, kappa and macro-F1). (report Figure 25)

parts: What it shows
The six-grade profile of each model as a polygon.
How to read it
Each axis is a metric (centre = 0). A larger polygon is better; dents show weak grades.
What we found
All polygons are large at grade 0 and dented at grade 3; most are also dented at grade 9 (F1 0.12–0.21), except RF (0.31).
What it means
The same grades are difficult for every model: the limitation lies in the data (overlapping grades, few grade-9 leaves), not in a particular method.
Say to the chairman
"Every model finds grade 0 easy and grades 3 and 9 hard."

blocks.caption: Predicted vs observed severity score of the best machine-learning and deep-learning models (black: mean ± SD per grade). (report Figure 26)

parts: What it shows
Predicted score against observed grade for RF and DNN-F1.
How to read it
Dots = leaves; black squares = mean prediction per grade ± SD; dashed = 1:1 line.
What we found
Mean predictions of RF rise steadily (1.20, 2.14, 3.28, 4.15, 4.88, 5.28 for grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9) but grade 0 is over-predicted and grades 7 and 9 under-predicted.
What it means
The order is right but extremes are pulled towards the middle (shrinkage), typical of regression on noisy labels. Leaves of grades 7 and 9 are under-estimated by about 2–4 grades.
Say to the chairman
"The score follows the right order but compresses the extremes."

blocks.text: 9. Steps 14–15: the covariate baseline and the comparison with LORO
9.1 Step 14 – Covariate baseline: what do the spectra add to the calendar?

Disease rose with crop age and date and differed with sowing time, variety and stage. A spectral model could therefore look accurate partly because it recognises the calendar rather than the disease (De Wolf and Isard, 2007). Step 14 builds models that know only the calendar, crop and weather – no spectrum – and credits the spectra only with what they add (Kuhn and Johnson, 2013; Zhang et al., 2014; Bijlwan et al., 2025).

rows: Step 14 – Covariate baseline M0, spectral model M1, combined model M2 (Step 2.5.5)
Measure how much of the disease the covariates explain without any sensor, and whether the leaf spectra add to it.

UNS-TRAIN: 1379 unsprayed leaves of the 25 unsprayed training plots (fitting and inner tuning). UNS-TEST: 573 unsprayed leaves of the 11 unsprayed test plots (evaluation). The 378 leaves of the sprayed healthy block are left out: they share every covariate with the unsprayed plots but are healthy because of the fungicide, so they would teach a false rule.
Covariates of Step 3 (DAS, DAS², timing, variety, stage code, 7-day weather, favourable days); DSF of Step 8 (spectra).

(1) Three inputs: covariates only; leaf spectra only (DSF of the task); spectra + covariates.
(2) Three models per input: B1 interpretable (logistic regression for A, proportional-odds ordinal logistic for B, linear regression with DAS and DAS² for C); random forest; B2 = the best ML model of Step 11 (SVM for A, XGBoost for B, RF for C).
(3) Standardise with the training statistics; tune RF, B2 and the logistic penalty in inner GroupKFold(3) by plot on UNS-TRAIN.
(4) Fit on UNS-TRAIN, predict UNS-TEST once.
(5) M0 = the stronger covariate-only model on the test leaves; M1 = B2 on spectra; M2 = B2 on spectra + covariates.
(6) Gains ΔS = M1 − M0, ΔC = M2 − M1, ΔT = M2 − M0 for macro-F1, AUC, balanced accuracy (A), macro-F1, QWK (B), R², RMSE (C).
(7) Paired plot bootstrap: resample the 11 unsprayed test plots 2000 times, recompute both models on the same resample, take the 2.5th–97.5th percentile of the difference. Real gain = interval excludes 0.
(8) DeLong test for the detection AUCs; B1 refitted on all unsprayed leaves with standardised covariates to show effect sizes (descriptive).
Seed 42; 2000 bootstrap resamples; weather windows end the day before sampling. With four dates, weather is collinear with date, so B1 uses DAS and DAS² as the time effect.

rows: Comparing two validation designs on the same data

A validation design is a way to estimate how accurate a model will be on new plots. LORO trains on two replications and tests on the third, three times, so every leaf is tested once; the 70:30 hold-out trains once on 70% of the plots and tests once on the other 30%. Both keep whole plots apart, so both are free of plot leakage.

A hold-out estimate depends on which plots happen to be in the test set, and with few test plots its variance is large; cross-validation averages over several test sets and uses every sample for testing (Kohavi, 1995; Molinaro et al., 2005; Vabalas et al., 2019; Xu and Goodacre, 2018). A higher 70:30 number is therefore an improvement only if it holds on the same leaves and across other 70:30 splits, not only for one lucky split.

All the numbers that define the analysis.
How to read it
To repeat the analysis exactly, keep every value; to adapt it, change only the value and the file named in the last column, and record the change.
What it means

With these settings and the seeds, a re-run on the same data reproduces the same split, the same features and the same models (the split search itself was re-run while writing this document and reproduced split.json exactly).
Say to the chairman
"Every setting is fixed and written down, so the analysis can be repeated exactly."

blocks.text: The core of the protocol in a few lines of Python
The listing shows the order of the essential operations of Steps 5, 8, 9 and 11 for one task and one model. It is a summary of the scripts, not a replacement for them.

lines: import numpy as np, pandas as pd, split_lib as SL
from alib import r2_maps, effective_ranges, shap_cars, corr_filter, relieff, vif_filter
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, GridSearchCV
from mlxtend.feature_selection import SequentialFeatureSelector as SFS
M = pd.read_csv("meta.csv")                                  # one row per leaf (Steps 2-4)
test_plots, info = SL.best_split(M, 0.30, seed=2026, n_cand=5000)   # Step 5
te = M["plot"].isin(test_plots).values; tr = ~te           # TEST is locked from here on
# Step 8 - selection on TRAIN only
Nm, Sm = r2_maps(R5[tr], y[tr]); used, thr = effective_ranges(Nm, Sm, w5)
ow = shap_cars(cand_bands[tr], y[tr], names, runs=20, n_iter=50, seed=42)["names"]
kept = corr_filter(IDX[tr], y[tr], 0.95)
w = relieff(IDX[kept].values[tr], y[tr], M["plot"].values[tr]); vi = top5(kept, w)
dsf = vif_filter(pd.concat([BANDS[ow], IDX[vi]], axis=1)[tr], 10.0)[0]
# Step 9 - inner folds, SFFS, grid search, refit (TRAIN only)
X = ALL[dsf].values; mu, sd = X[tr].mean(0), X[tr].std(0); Xs = (X - mu) / sd
inner = list(GroupKFold(3).split(Xs[tr], groups=M["plot"].values[tr]))
sfs = SFS(est, k_features=(1, 15), forward=True, floating=True, scoring="f1_macro", cv=inner).fit(Xs[tr], y[tr])
idx = smallest_subset_within_1pct(sfs.subsets_)
gs = GridSearchCV(est, grid, scoring="f1_macro", cv=inner).fit(Xs[tr][:, idx], y[tr])
model = gs.best_estimator_.fit(Xs[tr][:, idx], y[tr])
# Step 11 - the only use of TEST
pred = model.predict(Xs[te][:, idx])

blocks.label: Five rules that keep the analysis honest.
text: 1. Split by the unit whose samples are related (the plot), never by leaf.
2. Fix the split before any model is built, and never re-draw it after seeing results.
3. Everything that is chosen – features, subsets, settings, epochs, scaling – is chosen on the training plots.
4. Open the test plots once and report all models.
5. Report the uncertainty of the single split (plot bootstrap) and its luck (repeated splits), and test on an independent season or site.

blocks.text: 11. What the 70:30 analysis shows

items: **The disease signal is physical.** White rust lowers NIR reflectance, raises red and SWIR reflectance and moves the red-edge position 7.7 nm to shorter wavelengths (709.0 → 701.3 nm). The selected features sit on the green peak, the red edge, the NIR shoulder and the water-band edges.

**Detection is reliable on new plots** (SVM macro-F1 0.826, AUC 0.930); **six grades are limited** by the overlap of neighbouring grades (macro-F1 0.374, but 77% within one grade); **the score** explains half of the variation (R² 0.517, RMSE 1.92).
**Machine learning and deep learning perform alike** at leaf level; DT-EDNet and its attention modules have no spatial structure to use in a 4 × 4 pseudo-image.
**The spectra add severity information beyond the calendar** (+0.072 macro-F1, +0.102 R², real gains), while detection inside unsprayed plots is largely a matter of date.

**The design matters.** Grouped splitting is necessary (a leaf-level split would inflate six-grade macro-F1 by 0.055). The 70:30 models beat LORO on the same test leaves, partly because they saw plots of the same replication and partly because the main split was a favourable draw; over 20 splits the two designs are equal on average.

blocks.text: Limitations: one season and one site; subjective leaf grades; grade 9 small (132 leaves); growth stage confounded with date; networks trained with paper settings on CPU; no pre-symptomatic dates (Objective 3 not addressed). For the UAV phase the results support sensors covering the red edge (690–760 nm), the NIR shoulder (780–870 nm) and the SWIR water-band edges, keeping derivative features, and reporting detection plus a severity score or a few classes.
12. Questions the chairman may ask

blocks.q: Which leaves were used to choose the features of the models?
blocks.a: Only the 1631 leaves of the 33 training plots (Step 8). The feature lists of Objective 1 (Step 7) were computed on all leaves to describe the disease; the models never received them.

blocks.q: Is this a plot hold-out or a replication hold-out?
blocks.a: A plot hold-out: 15 whole plots (4 healthy, 11 unsprayed spread over R1–R3) are test plots. LORO, the earlier design, held out whole replications. Both keep the leaves of one plot together.

70:30 gives 15 test plots and 699 test leaves, enough for a plot bootstrap. 80:20 would leave only 9 test plots (2 healthy), so the estimate would be much less stable. A 20–30% test share is the usual rule (Gholamy et al., 2018).

blocks.q: How were the 15 test plots chosen? Could you have picked easy plots?
blocks.a: By fixed rules and a score based only on leaf counts, grades and dates – never on spectra or model results. Among 5000 rule-conforming candidates the most balanced one was taken (seed 2026). The repeated-split analysis shows that the chosen split happened to be a favourable one, and this is reported.

blocks.q: Where was the validation set for tuning?
blocks.a: Inside the training plots: inner GroupKFold(3) by plot for the machine-learning models (11 plots scored each time) and 11 validation plots for the early stopping of the networks. Effectively 47 : 23 : 30% for the networks.

blocks.q: Were the final models refitted on all data?
blocks.a: No. The delivered models are exactly the tested ones, trained on the training plots only, so their reported test accuracy applies to the files. (Some captions of the report said "all leaves"; this is corrected.)

blocks.q: Why is the uncertainty given as a bootstrap and not as a fold SD?
blocks.a: With one test set there are no folds. Whole test plots were resampled 1000 times (healthy and unsprayed separately), which keeps the leaves of a plot together (Field and Welsh, 2007).

On the same 699 leaves yes (17 of 30 comparisons really higher, none lower), but over 20 other 70:30 splits the two designs are equal on average. The 70:30 test plots have training plots of their own replication, which LORO does not allow.

blocks.q: What would you change if you repeated the analysis?
blocks.a: Use a pipeline object so that scaling is fitted inside each inner fold, a stratified grouped inner split, grouped splits also inside CARS, and report the repeated-split range together with the main split from the start.

blocks.q: How will you validate the models?
blocks.a: By applying the saved files, without retraining, to the 2026-27 leaf and UAV data and to the Bharatpur site, and comparing with the visual grades.

blocks.text: Glossary
**Hold-out** – one division of the data into a training set and a test set.
**Grouped split** – a split in which all samples of a group (here a plot) go to the same side.
**Stratified split** – a split that keeps the proportions of important classes (block types, grades, dates) in both sets.
**LORO** – leave-one-replication-out: train on two replications, test on the third, three times.
**Inner folds** – divisions of the training plots used to choose settings without touching the test plots.
**SFFS** – sequential floating forward selection: adds features one at a time and may drop one after each addition.
**Early stopping** – ending network training when the validation score stops improving.
**Plot bootstrap** – resampling whole test plots with replacement to estimate the uncertainty of a metric.
**Macro-F1** – mean F1 of all classes; every class counts equally.
**QWK** – quadratic weighted kappa; agreement that gives partial credit to near misses.
**RPD** – SD of the observed values divided by RMSE.
**Leakage** – information from the test data reaching the model, making accuracy look better than it is.
**DSF** – disease-specific feature set: optimal wavelengths + selected indices after VIF < 10.
